interactions.summary: The reading introduces the terrace of envy, where voices of love counteract envy, the eyelids of the penitents are sewn shut, and Sapia explains how rejoicing in others' harm led her here while prayer and penitence still make return possible.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Primary reading with minimal Jiang interruption

claims.claim: The terrace of envy is structured by countervailing voices of love and prayer, suggesting that envy is cured not only by pain but by a liturgy of reversed desire.
The sewn eyelids of the envious function as an image of forced inwardness: those who lived by looking sideways at others are deprived of sight in order to be remade.
Sapia's confession defines envy as rejoicing in another person's defeat more than in one's own good fortune, while also showing that charity from the living can still matter after death.

Dante the pilgrim distinguishes his own dangers by saying envy is not his deepest fear compared with the heavier punishments below, preserving a layered moral topography rather than flattening all sins together.

signature_moments.moment: The punishment of envy is given the harsh tactile image of iron wire sewing shut the eyelids.
signature_moments.source_phrase: iron wire pierces and sews up the lids
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is one of the poem's most memorable embodiments of a vice being turned against itself.

signature_moments.moment: Sapia names envy through the ugliness of rejoicing at others' harm.
signature_moments.source_phrase: I rejoiced far more at others' hurts than my own good fortune
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This gives the lecture a sharply defined case of envy before Jiang resumes interpretation.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture has now advanced from pride to envy, and the reading supplies a new set of embodied punishments and penitential logic for Jiang to interpret.
